gloss_terse: Amalekite — gentilic adjective/noun for a member of the Amalekite people, perennial enemies of Israel
gloss_readable: The gentilic עֲמָלֵקִי (Amaleqi) designates a member of the Amalekite nation, descendants of Esau's grandson Amalek who inhabited the Negev and Sinai wilderness. They served as Israel's archetypal enemy from the wilderness onward. The term appears collectively with the article for the nation alongside the Canaanites blocking Israel's entry (Num 14:25, 43, 45), in geographic references like 'the field of the Amalekites' (Gen 14:7), and for individuals such as the young man in Saul's campaigns (1 Sam 15:6; 30:13). Spanish 'amalecita' and Arabic 'عمالِقي' both preserve the gentilic form.

senses.1: Gentilic designating a member or the collective body of the Amalekite people, descendants of Esau's grandson Amalek. Used for the nation alongside the Canaanites (Num 14:25, 43, 45), in geographic references (Gen 14:7; Judg 12:15), and for individuals in Saul's campaigns (1 Sam 15:6; 30:13; 2 Sam 1:8, 13).

gloss_terse: Anah — Horite/Edomite personal name; discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing donkeys
gloss_readable: Anah (עָנָה) is a proper name in the Edomite-Horite genealogies of Genesis 36. The most notable bearer is the son of Zibeon who discovered the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing donkeys (Gen 36:24) -- a rare biographical detail in an otherwise formulaic list. This Anah is also father of Oholibamah, one of Esau's wives (Gen 36:2, 14, 18, 25). A second Anah appears as a son of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:20, 29; 1 Chr 1:38, 40), possibly the same figure from a different genealogical perspective. Spanish 'Ana' and Arabic 'عَنَاة' transliterate directly.

senses.1: An Edomite-Horite personal name. The primary bearer is the son of Zibeon who discovered hot springs while pasturing donkeys (Gen 36:24) and father of Esau's wife Oholibamah (Gen 36:2, 14, 18, 25). A second Anah appears as a son of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:20, 29; 1 Chr 1:38, 40).

gloss_terse: Barren, infertile — unable to bear children; of women and once of males and livestock; reversed by God
gloss_readable: The adjective עָקָר (aqar) describes the inability to produce offspring. It marks the most theologically significant women in Genesis: Sarah (Gen 11:30), Rebekah (Gen 25:21), and Rachel (Gen 29:31). The matriarchal barrenness motif underscores that covenant children come as divine gift, not natural expectation. Judges 13:2-3 applies it to Manoah's wife before Samson's birth, and Psalm 113:9 celebrates God settling 'the barren woman as a joyful mother.' Deuteronomy 7:14 extends the promise to both male and female, even livestock. Spanish 'esteril' and Arabic 'عاقِر' carry the same weight.

senses.1: Unable to bear children; infertile. Applied to the matriarchs Sarah (Gen 11:30), Rebekah (Gen 25:21), Rachel (Gen 29:31), and Manoah's wife (Judg 13:2-3), where barrenness sets up divine intervention. Extended to males and livestock (Deut 7:14; Exod 23:26). Used figuratively of personified Zion (Isa 54:1).

gloss_terse: Pahath-Moab — compound proper name ('governor of Moab') for a large post-exilic Judean clan in returnee lists
gloss_readable: Pahath-Moab (פַּחַת מוֹאָב) is a compound proper name meaning 'governor of Moab,' designating a prominent post-exilic Judean clan or its ancestral head. The name likely preserves the memory of a pre-exilic official who once served as governor over Moab during Judah's period of Transjordanian influence. The Pahath-Moab clan was one of the largest groups to return from Babylon: 2,812 members in Zerubbabel's return (Ezra 2:6; Neh 7:11) and additional members under Ezra (Ezra 8:4). Some of its men were among those who had married foreign wives and agreed to send them away (Ezra 10:30). Hashub son of Pahath-Moab helped repair the Jerusalem wall and the Tower of the Ovens (Neh 3:11), and the clan sealed the covenant renewal (Neh 10:14).

senses.1: Compound proper name meaning 'governor of Moab,' designating a large post-exilic Judean clan. Returned from Babylon with 2,812 members (Ezra 2:6; Neh 7:11), sent additional members with Ezra (Ezra 8:4), participated in foreign-wife reform (Ezra 10:30), and helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:11). Sealed the covenant renewal (Neh 10:14).

gloss_terse: Zobah — Aramean city-state in the Beqaa Valley region, whose king Hadadezer was defeated by David
gloss_readable: Zobah (צוֹבָה) identifies a powerful Aramean city-state in the Beqaa Valley region between Hamath and Damascus. It features prominently in David's wars, where Hadadezer king of Zobah is defeated at the Euphrates (2 Sam 8:3-5, 12; 1 Chr 18:3-9). The Ammonites hired Zobah's Arameans against David (2 Sam 10:6, 8), and Saul also fought Zobah's kings (1 Sam 14:47). After David's conquests, Rezon fled Zobah to establish a rival kingdom in Damascus (1 Kgs 11:23-24). Solomon subdued Hamath-Zobah (2 Chr 8:3). The compound 'Aram-Zobah' clarifies the Aramean identity.

senses.1: An Aramean city-state in the Beqaa Valley between Hamath and Damascus, ruled by Hadadezer. David defeated Hadadezer at the Euphrates (2 Sam 8:3-5, 12), the Ammonites hired Zobah's troops (2 Sam 10:6, 8), and Saul fought its kings (1 Sam 14:47). Rezon later fled to Damascus (1 Kgs 11:23-24); Solomon conquered Hamath-Zobah (2 Chr 8:3).

gloss_terse: Zalmunna — Midianite king captured and executed by Gideon alongside Zebah after the great rout
gloss_readable: Zalmunna (צַלְמֻנָּע) is the proper name of one of the two kings of Midian — always paired with Zebah — who were pursued, captured, and executed by Gideon following the decisive rout of the Midianite army. The name may derive from צֵל ('shadow') + מָנַע ('withhold'), perhaps meaning 'shade is withheld,' though its etymology remains uncertain. Gideon's pursuit of Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan, his encounter with the uncooperative men of Succoth and Penuel, and his personal execution of the two kings form one of the most vivid narratives in Judges 8:5-21. Psalm 83:12 invokes Zebah and Zalmunna as paradigmatic defeated enemies: 'Make their nobles like Zebah and Zalmunna.' Spanish 'Tsalmuná' and Swahili 'Salmuna' transliterate the name.

senses.1: One of two Midianite kings (always paired with Zebah) pursued across the Jordan, captured, and executed by Gideon as blood vengeance for his brothers slain at Tabor (Judg 8:5-21). Psalm 83:12 invokes Zebah and Zalmunna as paradigmatic defeated enemies. All twelve occurrences refer to the same individual.

gloss_terse: Kedar — second son of Ishmael; by extension, a powerful nomadic Arabian tribe known for black tents and flocks
gloss_readable: Kedar (קֵדָר) names the second son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29) and the nomadic Arabian tribe descended from him in the Syrian-Arabian desert. Renowned for their black goat-hair tents, the beloved compares her dark beauty to 'the tents of Kedar' (Song 1:5), while the psalmist laments dwelling among them as hostile exile (Ps 120:5). Isaiah prophesies Kedar's decline (Isa 21:16-17) yet envisions their flocks streaming to Jerusalem (Isa 60:7). Jeremiah records Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Kedar (Jer 49:28), and Ezekiel names them among Tyre's trading partners (Ezek 27:21).

senses.1: Ishmael's second son (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29) and the nomadic Arabian tribe descended from him. Known for black goat-hair tents (Song 1:5; Ps 120:5). Isaiah announces Kedar's decline (Isa 21:16-17) yet envisions their flocks serving Jerusalem (Isa 60:7). Jeremiah records Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against them (Jer 49:28); Ezekiel names them among Tyre's traders (Ezek 27:21).

gloss_terse: Kedesh — city of refuge in Naphtali; also cities in Issachar and southern Judah; name means 'sanctuary'
gloss_readable: Kedesh (קֶדֶשׁ), meaning 'sanctuary,' names up to three Israelite cities. The most prominent is Kedesh in Naphtali, a conquered Canaanite city (Josh 12:22) designated as a city of refuge (Josh 20:7) and Gershonite Levitical city (Josh 21:32; 1 Chr 6:61). Barak son of Abinoam was from Kedesh, where Deborah summoned him to fight Sisera (Judg 4:6, 9-10). Tiglath-pileser III captured it during the Assyrian conquest of Galilee (2 Kgs 15:29). A second Kedesh in Issachar (1 Chr 6:57) and a third in southern Judah (Josh 15:23) share the name.

senses.1: A city name meaning 'sanctuary,' primarily Kedesh in Naphtali -- a city of refuge (Josh 20:7) and Gershonite Levitical city (Josh 21:32). Home of Barak, where Deborah summoned him against Sisera (Judg 4:6, 9-10). Captured by Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kgs 15:29). Also a city in Issachar (1 Chr 6:57) and southern Judah (Josh 15:23).

gloss_terse: Thorn, thorn-bush — prickly plant; literally wilderness scrub, figuratively judgment and worthlessness
gloss_readable: The noun קוֹץ (qots) denotes thorns or thorn-bushes, one of Scripture's most versatile botanical images. Its foundational occurrence is in the primeval curse: 'thorns and thistles shall it bring forth' (Gen 3:18), establishing thorns as a sign of the ground's rebellion. Practically, Exodus 22:6 legislates when fire spreads through thorns to a neighbor's grain, and Gideon punishes the men of Succoth with 'thorns of the wilderness' (Judg 8:7, 16). Figuratively, thorns signal desolation (Isa 32:13), futile labor (Jer 12:13), wickedness (2 Sam 23:6), and enemies crackling like burning thorns (Ps 118:12).

senses.1: Thorns or thorn-bushes, used literally and figuratively. Introduced in the primeval curse (Gen 3:18, paired with 'thistles'). Practically: fire hazard (Exod 22:6), instruments of punishment (Judg 8:7, 16). Figuratively: desolation (Isa 32:13), futile labor (Jer 12:13), wickedness (2 Sam 23:6), enemies crackling like burning thorns (Ps 118:12), and hostile neighbors (Ezek 28:24).

gloss_terse: Ten thousand, myriad — large round number for counting people, valuables, or forces; late Aramaizing form
gloss_readable: The noun רִבּוֹ (ribbo) is a late Aramaizing synonym of רְבָבָה meaning 'ten thousand' or 'myriad,' appearing mostly in post-exilic literature. The returning exiles numbered 42,360 (Ezra 2:64; Neh 7:66), and temple treasury offerings are tallied in units of ribbo (1 Chr 29:7; Ezra 2:69; Neh 7:70-72). Daniel uses the plural for apocalyptic military forces casting down myriads (Dan 11:12). The dual ribbotayim in Psalm 68:18 means 'twice ten thousand' -- twenty thousand chariots of God. Spanish 'diez mil,' Arabic 'رَبْوَات,' and Korean '만' all render the concept.

senses.1: The numeral ten thousand or myriad, a late Aramaizing synonym of רְבָבָה. Used for census totals of returning exiles (Ezra 2:64; Neh 7:66), temple treasury tallies (1 Chr 29:7; Ezra 2:69), Nineveh's population (Jonah 4:11), apocalyptic military forces (Dan 11:12), and God's twenty thousand chariots in the dual form (Ps 68:18).
